title: Weekly Log: 第2周 05-08-2026
summary: Focusing on machine learning fundamentals, Hands-On Machine Learning reading, WEKA, and planning a Smart Clothing Organizer IoT project.
content:
This week was a bit more focused on learning than building. I spent most of my free time reading about machine learning, catching up with university work, and planning another project for the IoT Club. I didn't finish as many projects as last week, but I definitely learnt a lot.

1. Learning Machine Learning

This week I finally started reading Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras & TensorFlow by Aurélien Géron. It's a book that I've been meaning to start for a while now, and I've currently completed 39 out of 564 pages.

The chapters I've read so far focus more on understanding the different types of machine learning rather than immediately jumping into coding. It explains where each learning method is used, how they differ from one another, and introduces a lot of the terminology that's used throughout machine learning.

I liked that the book doesn't assume you already know everything. It starts from the basics and slowly builds up, which makes it a lot easier to understand before getting into actual implementations.

2. University Work

A lot of this week also went into university assignments and NPTEL work.

Since deadlines were getting closer, I decided to spend more time finishing assignments instead of starting another side project. Nothing particularly exciting here, but it feels good getting everything out of the way before moving on to bigger projects again.

3. Learning WEKA

Along with the book, I also started learning WEKA.

WEKA is a machine learning software developed by the University of Waikato that lets you experiment with machine learning algorithms through a graphical interface instead of writing code. You can import datasets, preprocess them, train different models, visualize results and compare algorithms all in one place.

Since I'm still learning machine learning itself, it was nice being able to actually see these algorithms running instead of only reading about them.

4. New IoT Club Project

We've also started planning our next IoT Club project, which is a Smart Clothing Organizer.

The idea is to build a smart wardrobe that can automatically bring the clothing item you're looking for to the front. Instead of searching through your closet, you simply choose the item from a mobile app, and the organizer moves it into view while an LED points directly at it.

We're also planning to add quite a few extra features like filtering clothes based on the weather or occasion, detecting missing clothes in the organizer, laundry reminders, voice commands and even gesture controls that let you shuffle through clothes with a wave of your hand.

It's still in the planning stage, so there's a lot of hardware and software to figure out, but I think it'll be a really fun project to build.

5. Typing Speed Tester

I'm still working on the Python typing speed tester that I mentioned in my last blog.

I haven't had enough time to properly work on it this week because of university assignments, but I'm slowly adding more features whenever I get some free time. Hopefully I'll have it finished soon.

6. Tool of the Week

This week's interesting discovery was OmniRoute.

OmniRoute is an open-source AI gateway that connects different AI coding tools and model providers through a single endpoint. Instead of configuring every AI tool separately, OmniRoute handles everything in the background and routes requests to whichever provider you're using.

One feature I thought was really cool is that it supports tools like Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot, Codex and Cline, while also automatically switching providers if one becomes unavailable or reaches its limits. It also includes features like smart routing and token compression, which makes it a pretty useful project if you regularly work with AI coding assistants.

I'll probably spend some more time experimenting with it over the next week.

That's pretty much how this week went. It wasn't as project-heavy as last week, but I got a much better understanding of machine learning, learnt a new tool, discovered another useful open-source project, and started planning what will probably become my biggest IoT project so far.

title: Weekly Log: 第1周 27-07-2026
summary: Sunday Quiz maker with Tkinter, IoT Phantom Gate safety system, OpenCV shredded document reassembly capstone, and LeetCode SQL/BFS.
content:
Had a pretty productive week working on a few projects and diving deeper into some computer science topics.

1. Sunday Quiz Project Reveal

My friend and I do this thing where we pick a mini project, build it separately during the week without showing each other, and then reveal what we made on Sunday to learn Python together.

This week’s project was a quiz maker. Instead of just doing a basic text quiz in the terminal, I wanted to support different question types (like multiple choice, fill-in-the-blank, and images).

I used Tkinter and PIL so that whenever an image question pops up (like identifying an animal), a separate window opens with the picture, and then closes when you move on. I also added a simple hint trigger.

Here’s how I handled opening the image popups:

def show_image_window(image_path):
    if not os.path.exists(image_path):
        print(f"⚠️ Warning: Could not find image file '{image_path}'. Skipping image display.")
        return None

    img_window = tk.Toplevel()
    img_window.title("Question Image")
    
    raw_img = Image.open(image_path)
    raw_img.thumbnail((300, 300))
    quiz_img = ImageTk.PhotoImage(raw_img)
    
    img_label = tk.Label(img_window, image=quiz_img)
    img_label.image = quiz_img  # Reference to avoid garbage collection
    img_label.pack(padx=10, pady=10)
    
    img_window.update()
    return img_window

It was fun seeing how differently both of us built the exact same thing on Sunday. Next week we’re making a typing speed tester.

2. IoT Expothon: Phantom Gate

I’m also working on an IoT Expothon project called Phantom Gate – AI-Based Smart Industrial Safety & Access Control System.

It’s essentially a tabletop maze setup where judges turn a rotary encoder to move a payload through a grid. The catch is that the grid has invisible optical beam sensors. If someone breaks a beam, the system:

  • Triggers an emergency E-STOP
  • Snaps a photo of their face
  • Plays a voice alert ("INTRUDER DETECTED")
  • Sends an emergency SMS to a phone

There's a lot of hardware and sensor logic involved, but it's going to be cool to test out physically.

3. Capstone Project: Document Reassembly with OpenCV

I also built a capstone project focused on automated document reassembly using OpenCV and computer vision. The idea is simple but tricky in practice: if you feed it images of shredded paper strips, jigsaw pieces of a document, or torn receipts, the system analyzes the edges, contours, and text/line continuations to piece them back together into the original document. It was a really fun challenge working through the image processing pipeline and matching logic to get the fragments aligning correctly.

4. LeetCode SQL & BFS

MySQL on LeetCode: I just realized LeetCode has dedicated MySQL problem sets! Diving straight into database queries alongside standard DSA problems is going to make practicing SQL so much more structured.

Graph Algorithms (BFS): I spent time mastering the theory and code for Breadth-First Search (BFS). Understanding queue-based level-order traversal opens up so many pathfinding possibilities, and I’m ready to start applying it to graph-based problems soon.

5. Course Realities & Cool Finds

Pivot on NPTEL: I started my NPTEL coursework this week, but to be completely honest, the lectures aren't landing well for me. Instead of slogging through material that isn't sticking, I’m taking full ownership of my learning path and switching to curated self-study resources.

6. Tool of the Week

I stumbled upon Chai Visual ("Learn CS by watching it move"). Watching data structures, pointers, and memory step through frame-by-frame makes complex algorithm logic click instantly. Highly recommended if you're a visual learner.

Onward to next week's typing speed build and Phantom Gate prototyping!
